items.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998
items.q: call my old pals, you know, like Sonny Burke at Decca and Paul Weston was at Columbia Records

ctx.x: Well you know, you ask very good questions by the way. Up to that point that you’re talking about, when you started hearing my music, I wasn’t before that, prior to that, like when I went through the quote big band era, where I played with the bands like the first big band I played with was Bunny Berigan in 1938. I played trombone and arranged music as well for the band. Then I did the same thing with the Bob Crosby band in 1939, and then I went with the Artie Shaw band in 1940. And now from ‘40 through ‘45 I…

And bop was kind of supposed to be a floating type of rhythm on top cymbals and stuff. You weren’t supposed to hear it, you were supposed to feel it here. You were supposed to feel what he was trying — and I don’t know, I never felt that, so I said, “Hey you know, Harry, I just don’t feel that kind of music,” and you know, “maybe it’s time you got another boy.” And his jaw dropped. He looked at me and he couldn’t believe what I was saying. And he said, “well, okay.” So I left the band. For two years I thought all…

them — I picked songs, and by arithmetic I went back the number of years, the age group I was trying to hit was 18-35 in the market. So I went back, when were those 18 to 35 year olds hearing, “ooooh would you like to take a walk” with the little girl down the street, or the boy you know, and so by arithmetic I picked songs from the top ten of those years. And that’s what “S’ Wonderful,” “S’ Marvelous,” “S’ Awful Nice.” So in other words I didn’t change my style of writing that much. I still wrote for brass and…
